faq.a: It is when water in rock cracks freezes and expands, widening the cracks, then thaws and seeps deeper. Repeated many times, it breaks rocks apart. It is also called frost wedging.

faq.q: Why does ice take up more space than water?
faq.a: When water freezes, its molecules lock into an open, honeycomb-like pattern that takes up about 9 percent more space than liquid water. That is why ice floats and pipes can burst in winter.
asks: Why does water expand when it freezes?

faq.q: Why are there piles of broken rock under cliffs?
faq.a: Freeze-thaw breaks pieces off the cliff face, and they fall and collect at the bottom in sloping piles called scree or talus.
In places where the temperature often crosses freezing, like mountains and cold regions in spring and autumn. In places always frozen or never frozen, it hardly happens.
asks: Does freeze-thaw happen in the Arctic?

faq.a: Water gets into cracks in roads, freezes and expands, breaking up the surface. Traffic then knocks out the loose pieces, making potholes, often after winter.
asks: Why are there more potholes after winter?

facts: Water expands by about 9 percent when it freezes.
Scree slopes form from rock fragments broken off by freeze-thaw weathering.
